meters.label: Requests per second slow or dropped

frames.narration: A quiet evening: 100 requests per second spread over 2 instances. Each can serve 100, so each runs at 50%. The policy is target tracking at 60%, with a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 20 instances.
A promotion goes out. Traffic jumps to 400 rps within a minute: 200% of what 2 instances can serve. The load balancer keeps sending it all, so requests queue, slow down and some fail.
The fleet reports its load to the metrics system, which averages it per minute. The autoscaler reads it: at 60% target it needs ceil(400 / 60) = 7 instances.

The autoscaler launches 5 instances. They boot, pull the image and warm caches, which takes 2 minutes, and they receive no traffic until then. A 2 minute cooldown starts so it does not launch again before it sees the result.
Traffic keeps climbing to 1000 rps while the new instances warm. Only 2 are ready, serving 200 rps, so about 800 rps are slow or dropped. This lag, not the policy, is the damage.

The 5 instances are ready: 7 serve 700 rps of 1000, still 143% load. The autoscaler now wants ceil(1000 / 60) = 17 and launches 10 more, another 2 minute wait. A bigger spike hits the 20 maximum and stays overloaded.
17 instances are ready and share 1000 rps at about 59% each. The spike is absorbed, about 5 minutes after it began. Warming instances were billed the whole time they were useless.

The spike fades to 300 rps: 17 instances sit at 18%. Scale-in is deliberately slower than scale-out: after 5 calm minutes it removes one instance at a time. Scaling in hard, then having to scale out again through a 2 minute warm-up, is flapping.
At night, 80 rps needs only 2 instances at 40% load. The autoscaler stops at the minimum of 2, which keeps a safe floor and lets one instance fail without an outage.
